title: The Last Letter
premise: Ines Iversen, a courier carrying sealed diplomatic codes for a republic on the brink of surrender, hides in plain sight as a bookbinder's apprentice in a besieged port city. When an unknown woman leaves a child at the workshop door with a note reading 'forget my face,' Ines discovers the child carries half of a cipher that could either secure a favorable armistice or hand the city to its conquerors. Racing to complete the diplomatic work before the signing, Ines must choose between delivering the codes that preserve their own survival and exposing the truth that could save thousands. The novel ends with Ines finishing the mission as the workshop burns, delivering the last letter not to the ministers but to the child, who will carry the republic's memory into whatever comes after.
about_author: Silas Okafor is a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing the private correspondence of collapsed governments before turning to fiction. He writes from a small coastal town, drawn always to the people history forgets to name.

chapters.title: The Weight of Sealed Things
chapters.summary: Ines Iversen arrives in the port city of Vellmark under a false trade license, the diplomatic codes sewn into a ledger binding. POV: Ines. The emotional beat is wary competence — a professional assessing how many days the republic has left, and pretending not to care.

chapters.title: Glue, Thread, and Silence
chapters.summary: Ines settles into Master Aldric's bindery, learning the rhythms of the workshop while mapping which officials still answer their doors. POV: Ines. The beat is cautious belonging — the dangerous comfort of routine in a city already rehearsing its surrender.

chapters.title: The Child at the Door
chapters.summary: A woman leaves a six-year-old named Tam on the workshop step at dawn with a note: 'forget my face.' Inside Tam's coat lining, Ines finds a cipher fragment matching her own codes. POV: Ines. The beat is dread — the low profile she built is now impossible.

chapters.title: What the Ministers Paid For
chapters.summary: Ines deciphers enough to learn the fragments together form the armistice terms' authentication key — forgeable by whoever holds both halves. POV: Ines, with a flashback to her handler's final warning. The beat is cold clarity about what she's actually carrying.

chapters.title: Aldric's War
chapters.summary: Master Aldric reveals he once bound documents for the old regime and recognizes the paper stock of the cipher fragment — it came from a ministry print run, meaning someone inside sent the child. POV: Aldric. The beat is guilt resurfacing after thirty years of quiet complicity.

chapters.title: The Man Who Counts Doors
chapters.summary: Colonel Vessane, the occupying force's liaison, begins inspecting workshops for 'unregistered presses,' lingering too long at the bindery. POV: Vessane. The beat is patient menace — power enjoying the theater of legality before dropping the mask.

chapters.title: Tam Learns to Fold
chapters.summary: Waiting out the inspections, Ines teaches Tam paper-folding; the child reproduces a fold pattern only someone raised in the ministry nursery would know. POV: Ines. The beat is reluctant tenderness hardening into resolve — the child is evidence, and evidence gets destroyed.

chapters.title: Half a Key Is a Weapon
chapters.summary: Ines makes contact with Deputy Minister Corvain, expecting an ally, and realizes he wants her fragment not to sign the armistice but to alter it in his faction's favor. POV: Ines. The beat is disillusionment — duty, she sees, is just someone else's ambition wearing a uniform.

chapters.title: The Night the Harbor Burned
chapters.summary: Vessane's forces torch the harbor warehouses as reprisal for partisan sabotage; the city watches its own livelihood burn. POV: multiple brief vignettes through the workshop's windows. The beat is collective grief and the first open question of whether survival is worth the price.

chapters.title: Correspondence in a Dead Language
chapters.summary: Aldric shows Ines letters he bound for the old regime — proof Vessane was once the regime's own informer, now selling the same city twice. POV: Aldric. The beat is bitter vindication that changes nothing: knowing a man's corruption is not the same as being free of him.

chapters.title: The Price Quoted in Bread
chapters.summary: Food runs out; Vessane offers rations to any household that reports hidden documents. Neighbors begin looking at the bindery differently. POV: Ines. The beat is siege morality — hunger making collaborators of ordinary people, and Ines understanding she may be the reason they starve.

chapters.title: Forget My Face
chapters.summary: The woman returns briefly at night — Tam's mother, a ministry clerk — and explains she stole the fragment to stop Corvain but can't be seen again. POV: the mother, Marta. The beat is desperate maternal sacrifice, asking a stranger to love her child enough to lie forever.

chapters.title: Two Halves, One Hand
chapters.summary: Marta's fragment and Ines's are reunited; completed, the key authenticates the original armistice terms — decent ones, drafted before the factions began carving. POV: Ines. The beat is terrible responsibility: one courier now holds the difference between mercy and plunder.

chapters.title: Vessane's Invitation
chapters.summary: Vessane summons Ines openly, revealing he knows what she carries and offering her passage out in exchange for the key — his price for letting the workshop stand. POV: Ines. The beat is temptation sharpened to a point: survival offered explicitly in exchange for everyone else's future.

chapters.title: The Apprentice Who Wasn't
chapters.summary: Aldric covers for Ines during a search, destroying his own masterworks to hide the cipher in plain rebinds, and is arrested in Ines's place. POV: Aldric, in custody. The beat is redemption purchased late — a man finally choosing a side, at the cost of everything he kept safe for thirty years.

chapters.title: What Survivors Owe
chapters.summary: Ines must decide: flee with Tam using Vessane's passage, or finish the delivery and authenticate the true terms before the signing in four days. POV: Ines. The beat is the novel's moral hinge — the price of survival weighed against the debt owed to those who won't survive.

chapters.title: The Long Way Through the Quarantine Quarter
chapters.summary: Ines moves through the plague-quarantined slums where no soldier patrols, carrying both fragments and Tam, toward the neutral chancery where the signing will occur. POV: Ines. The beat is grim pilgrimage — the city's forgotten people silently aiding the courier because she is carrying something for all of them.

chapters.title: Corvain's Signature
chapters.summary: At the chancery, Ines interrupts Corvain presenting forged terms; she produces the authenticated key and the original draft, exposing him before the assembled delegates. POV: Ines. The beat is quiet triumph without safety — truth spoken aloud in a room full of men deciding whether to hear it.

chapters.title: The Workshop Still Stands
chapters.summary: Vessane, exposed as a double seller by the same records, orders the bindery burned anyway as spite; Ines arrives too late to save the building but pulls Aldric from custody in the chaos. POV: alternating Ines and Aldric. The beat is loss and rescue entangled — the climax's cost made real.

chapters.title: Armistice
chapters.summary: The true terms are signed; the city surrenders with its archives, its names, and its dead accounted for rather than erased. POV: Ines, watching from the crowd. The beat is hollow relief — victory measured in what was prevented, never in what was saved.

chapters.title: The Last Letter
chapters.summary: Ines writes down everything — the codes, the names, Marta's face described in loving detail so Tam might someday find her — and seals it for Tam to open when grown. POV: Ines. The beat is grief transmuted into inheritance; memory as the only country left to give.

chapters.title: After the Republic
chapters.summary: One year later, Ines and Tam live quietly in a border town, binders again; a letter arrives bearing Marta's handwriting. POV: Tam, reading over Ines's shoulder. The beat is earned hope — survival repaid at last, not as escape but as reunion, with the past finally allowed to catch up gently.
